newsitem.title: FRANCE: Credit Lyonnais board to examine restructuring plan.
newsitem.headline: Credit Lyonnais board to examine restructuring plan.

text.p: The board of Credit Lyonnais will hold a special meeting on Thursday to examine a plan aimed at getting the state-controlled bank ready for privatisation and putting its money-losing past behind it.

The plan, submitted to the centre-right government last month, is the basis for intense negotiations between Credit Lyonnais and the finance ministry about the bank's recapitalisation needs for attracting a buyer.

The extraordinary meeting of the board composed of industry figures such as Jean-Luc Lagardere, chairman of magazines to missiles group Lagardere and government representatives would be an "information" session, a bank official said. There would be no statement afterward, he said.
Credit Lyonnais is still recovering from wild expansion in the late 1980s that briefly made it the largest bank outside Japan before nearly bringing about its collapse.
Bank and government officials have said the recovery plan puts no figure on the bank's cash requirements.

But the sum most persistently mentioned in media reports is 12 billion francs ($2.3 billion), the amount bank chairman Jean Peyrelevade said last year was needed to boost its solvency ratios to acceptable levels to be successfully privatised.
The government, which bailed out the bank in 1994 and 1995 and gave it emergency aid last year, has agreed to pump more money into bank to ready it for sale but must decide on the sum.

Those close to the ministry talks said they were going well. But a government official acknowledged France had "fallen behind on our schedule" in submitting the recovery plan to the European Commission which must approve any fresh state aid.

The official said the plan would be given as soon as possible to the Commission, which warned on Tuesday it would have to get a look at it soon or it would be unable to approve new help before the bank's 1996 accounts close in March.

The announcement of the latest rescue plan had been expected to coincide with the bank's 1996 results. A source close to the ministry talks said, however, it could be "two, three or four weeks" before the Commission sees it. The Commission said it should have received the plan before the end of last year.

Calculating the bank's recapitalisation needs is complicated by what disposals the bank makes. Many assets were bought at peak prices and would trigger capital losses if sold now and that could affect its solvability ratios.
But the Commission has been pressing the bank to step up its sale programme to comply with the conditions of its 1995 rescue.
Analysts have said the final bill to French taxpayers from the Credit Lyonnais saga could top 100 billion francs, making it one of the world's biggest banking fiascos.
Even with the rescue plan and despite the government's stated aim of a fast sale, the bank has said it does not expect to be in shape to be privatised until 1998.
The bank limped back into profit in 1995 after losses of 21 billion between 1992 and 1994 and Peyrelevade has said he would be satisfied if it broke even for 1996. ($1=5.307 French Franc)
